stories.title: Trump orders contractors to run congressional requests past the White House
stories.summary: An executive order signed Nov. 21 tells federal contractors to alert the White House to congressional requests and withhold material it calls privileged.
story: President Trump signed an executive order on Friday, Nov. 21, requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to tell the White House about congressional information requests and to coordinate their answers with the administration. CNN, NPR and NBC News report that it directs contractors to follow White House and agency instructions on withholding communications treated as executive privilege. Companies that do not comply could lose existing contracts or be suspended from future work. The White House says the aim is protecting executive privilege from congressional overreach (CNN, NPR, Fox News).

The order follows a memo from White House counsel Will Scharf requiring agencies to approve officials' testimony before Congress. It arrives weeks before Democrats, who won both chambers on Nov. 3, take over committees in January and begin planned investigations of the administration and the Trump family's business dealings. Trump also moved Stephen Miller into the chief of staff job, replacing Susie Wiles, and Fox News describes that move as a shift toward governing without Congress.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, who will chair House Judiciary, called the order "unprecedented and blatantly unlawful" and later said it has "all the force of an interoffice memo," according to CNN. Rep. Robert Garcia called it a "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." Former U.S. attorney Joyce Vance argued executive privilege protects internal deliberations, not commercial dealings. The Hill reports contractors are now caught in the crossfire of coming Democratic probes.

Legal analysts quoted by CNN note that courts have held executive privilege is not absolute. The dispute could land in court once committees start issuing subpoenas, with Democratic investigations of contracts tied to the White House ballroom among those expected.
facts: Trump signed the order Friday, Nov. 21, 2026.
It covers all federal contractors and subcontractors, tens of thousands of businesses.
Noncompliance could mean contract termination or suspension from future federal work.
Raskin and Garcia, both Democrats, call the order unlawful.
Democrats take House committee gavels in January.
stories.next: Watch for the first committee subpoena to a contractor in January and any court challenge to the order.
stories.left: Congress has a constitutional duty to check the executive, and the order tries to chill private companies from answering lawful requests. Executive privilege covers the president's own deliberations, not the commercial records of firms that sell to the government. Threatening contracts over compliance with Congress looks like intimidation timed to blunt the investigations voters just authorized.
stories.right: Presidents of both parties have guarded confidential executive communications, and contractors often hold documents that reveal internal deliberations. A uniform process to flag privileged material is a reasonable way to avoid accidental waiver. Conservative writers also note that Trump has said he is open to working with Democrats on health care, immigration, college sports and film tax credits, which they read as a sign he wants deals alongside the fights (Washington Examiner).
stories.flag: Raskin's remark that the order has the force of an interoffice memo is his characterization, not a court finding.

stories.title: Huang faces two congressional appearances as Trump floats a pardon he says isn't needed
stories.summary: Huang is due for a closed-door House interview Dec. 1 and a Senate Banking hearing Dec. 3, while lawmakers in both parties question his return.
story: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, Nov. 23, and the stock jumped about 31%, according to CNBC. Trump told CNBC "I made the deal," saying he pressed the board. On Wednesday CNBC, citing the New York Post, reported that Trump said he would be willing to pardon Huang if needed but did not think it would be "necessary," and that Huang should not invoke the Fifth Amendment.

Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1, and he will testify publicly as the sole witness before Senate Banking on Dec. 3 in a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls," CNBC reports. Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, scheduled the hearing hours after the reinstatement. Sen. Elizabeth Warren is expected to chair the committee in January.

Criticism has been bipartisan. Rep. Don Bacon told CNBC the decision was "a failure of character." Fox News reports Sen. Tom Cotton said the move does not resolve concerns about chip smuggling and remote access by China, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune pledged vigorous oversight and bipartisan export-control legislation. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries wants "ironclad" export controls in the defense bill (Washington Examiner). Former Vice President Mike Pence called for a congressional probe (The Hill).
Trump's clemency power covers only federal offenses, CNBC notes, so a pardon would not reach state matters such as the California attorney general's subpoena covered earlier this month.
facts: The board reinstated Huang Monday, Nov. 23; Nvidia rose about 31% that day.
House closed-door interview: Dec. 1. Senate Banking public hearing: Dec. 3.
Trump says he pressed the board and would pardon Huang if needed, per the New York Post via CNBC.
Bacon, Cotton, Warren and Jeffries have all criticized the reinstatement.
Nvidia fell 5.86% Tuesday to $155.38.
stories.next: Huang's House interview on Dec. 1 and Senate Banking hearing on Dec. 3.
stories.left: A president leaning on a company's board to restore a CEO under investigation, while floating a pardon, is the kind of transactional politics that breeds corruption. Democrats say the questions are about export-control compliance and whether chips reached China's military. They want sworn answers and statutory limits, not reassurance.
stories.right: China hawks in the GOP are as angry as Democrats, and they argue the issue is national security, not partisanship. Cotton and Bacon want the chip-smuggling and remote-access questions answered under oath and tougher export law. Some conservatives defend the markets' relief and say an innocent-until-proven-guilty standard should apply to Huang until investigators show wrongdoing.
stories.flag: Bacon's claim that Huang was compromised by a Chinese spy is his allegation; no charges have been reported.

stories.title: Schumer says he has the votes as Van Hollen's challenge heads to a Dec. 1 secret ballot
stories.summary: Schumer says he has locked up the 28 votes needed, while Van Hollen calls the race wide open ahead of the Dec. 1 caucus vote.
story: Senate Democrats choose their leader by secret ballot on Dec. 1, and a candidate needs 28 votes, The Hill reports. Chris Van Hollen formally entered the race on Nov. 12 to challenge Chuck Schumer, who has led the caucus since 2017. The Hill reports that Schumer says he has secured the necessary votes, while Van Hollen says it is still a "wide-open race."

Public endorsements may not predict the secret ballot. Newsweek counted 16 senators publicly behind Schumer and four behind Van Hollen, while The Hill earlier counted 15 public Schumer backers to five for Van Hollen. Many senators have not declared. It is the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades.

An Economist/YouGov poll reported by The Hill found 50% of respondents view Schumer unfavorably, even after Democrats won the House and Senate on Nov. 3. Fox News reports Schumer is leaning on an early advantage, while Van Hollen warns against a coronation. Rahm Emanuel urged Schumer to serve only one more term (The Hill). Trump said working with Schumer would be difficult, calling him "one of the worst" Senate leaders "in history."
The Hill also reports senators are pressing Schumer to give the caucus more control over the agenda, a sign that even a win may come with conditions.
facts: Vote date: Dec. 1, secret ballot.
28 votes are needed to win.
Van Hollen entered the race Nov. 12.
An Economist/YouGov poll found 50% view Schumer unfavorably.
Public counts differ: Newsweek has 16 for Schumer and four for Van Hollen.
stories.next: The caucus vote on Dec. 1; the margin will show how much of the caucus wants a new direction.
stories.left: Progressives argue that a party with a base this disenchanted needs a fresh leader who will fight harder on Trump's agenda, the Iran war and affordability. Van Hollen's backers say a leadership change would signal that the midterm win is a mandate to confront the White House, not to manage it. Schumer's allies reply that experience and caucus unity matter most when Democrats are about to take back committee gavels.
stories.right: Conservatives see a party arguing over how far left to move after its win, and they expect either result to keep Democrats focused on confrontation with Trump. Some on the right say the base's 50% unfavorable rating for Schumer shows Democrats still lack a message beyond opposition. Republicans also note Trump's view that Schumer is a hard negotiating partner, which shapes any shutdown or spending talks.

stories.title: California prosecutors ask the state Supreme Court to stop Newsom's death-row commutations
stories.summary: Prosecutors from 29 counties say Newsom skipped required victim notice; his reply is due Dec. 4 and Bonta says nothing will be formal until the court acts.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he would commute all 548 California death sentences to life without parole. District attorneys from 29 counties then asked the California Supreme Court to halt the plan, arguing he did not give crime victims a chance to be heard, according to CalMatters and NBC News. A separate group, the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, also sued.

Newsom's office argues the notice requirement does not apply when a governor acts on his own initiative without an application. Because 382 of the cases involve prisoners with more than one felony conviction, the court must weigh in on those, CalMatters reports. Briefs were due Nov. 24 and Newsom's response is due Dec. 4. Attorney General Rob Bonta told the court Newsom will not formally commute any sentences until the justices act.

The California District Attorneys Association said the decision makes no distinction among crimes, offenders or victims, and a victim's father called it a betrayal (NBC News, Fox News). Some prosecutors, including in Los Angeles, Riverside and Orange counties, say they will keep seeking death sentences where law allows. Santa Clara County DA Jeff Rosen backed Newsom, and the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers called the move a "decision of historic moral clarity and courage" (NBC News).

Trump has criticized the move and announced a federal directive to seek death sentences in some child-murder cases, the Washington Examiner reports, but he has no authority to reverse state commutations.
facts: Newsom announced the plan Nov. 5, covering 548 sentences.
29 county DAs filed a petition Monday, Nov. 23.
Newsom's reply to the court is due Dec. 4.
Bonta says no sentence will be formally commuted before the court acts.
Voters rejected repeal initiatives in 2012 and 2016.
stories.next: Newsom's Dec. 4 response to the California Supreme Court.
stories.left: Newsom says a system that cannot be administered fairly should not carry out executions, and that picking some sentences to commute would create two classes of victims. Supporters point to wrongful-conviction risk, racial disparities and decades of delay. They say lifelong imprisonment gives families certainty, and note some survivors and prosecutors back the move.
stories.right: Voters rejected repeal twice, in 2012 and 2016, and prosecutors say one governor cannot erase jury verdicts in a single stroke. Victims' families argue they were promised a hearing and were not given one. Even supporters of clemency in individual cases say the process matters, and a blanket order skips the case-by-case review the law contemplates.

stories.title: San Francisco braces for a king-tide peak near 11 a.m. as a storm hits Thanksgiving travel
stories.summary: The NWS forecasts 8.8 feet at 10:49 a.m. Wednesday in San Francisco, with Lurie planning for 9 feet; the Posey Tube stays closed through Friday.
story: The highest tide of the week arrives Wednesday morning. The National Weather Service forecast a peak of 8.8 feet at 10:49 a.m. in San Francisco, about 3 feet above normal, the Chronicle reports. Mayor Daniel Lurie said the city is planning for a high-water mark of 9 feet, which would top the previous record of about 8.7 feet. KQED reports Tuesday's tide already broke the November record.

A coastal flood warning covers Monday through Thanksgiving Day, NBC News and CNN report, and an incoming storm adds roughly another 6 inches of water. The Port erected a mile of flood barriers along the waterfront for the first time, and the Chronicle lists the Embarcadero, Ocean Beach, Treasure Island and the Highway 260 Posey and Webster tubes among likely flood spots. Oakland's Posey Tube is closed Sunday through Friday as a precaution.

Lurie asked residents to avoid travel unless essential through Wednesday afternoon. SFO said it no longer expects ground stops because of flooding, according to the Chronicle. Forecasters caution that wind, waves and El Niño-raised sea levels could make water on the ground 1 to 4 feet higher than predicted. Lurie also said worse king tides are expected Christmas week and in January.
In Fremont, Open-Meteo data on the site shows rain likely today, with a high of 64 and a low of 51, and more rain Sunday.
facts: Forecast peak: 8.8 feet at 10:49 a.m. Wednesday (NWS, via the Chronicle).
Lurie is planning for 9 feet; the record is about 8.7 feet.
Coastal flood warning runs Monday through Thanksgiving Day.
The Posey Tube is closed Sunday through Friday.
Higher king tides are expected Christmas week and in January.
stories.next: Post-peak damage reports Wednesday afternoon, then the next big tides at Christmas.
stories.left: Climate-adaptation advocates say these tides preview a costly future for low-lying Bay shoreline, and CalMatters asks whether California is ready. They want sea-wall and wetland money steered to the communities hit first, and they note that Lurie himself warned worse tides are coming at Christmas and in January.
stories.right: Conservatives generally stress local preparedness over climate framing, and note the event stacks several causes: a king tide, a storm and an El Niño year. They say the immediate test is whether emergency crews and flood barriers hold, and they favor practical flood-control spending over broad climate mandates.
stories.flag: All tide heights are forecasts. No post-peak report confirming the actual Wednesday level had been found.

stories.title: Iran says three tankers hit mines under U.S. escort as Washington widens sanctions
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says three tankers hit mines in Hormuz despite U.S. cover; Treasury sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses.
story: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said three oil tankers suffered explosions and fires after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, even though all three were under U.S. military air cover and escort, CNBC reports. CNN reports that attacks on shipping in and around the strait are at their highest level since the war began. Oil settled up more than $2 on Tuesday as traders weighed the attacks (CNBC).

On Monday the Treasury announced sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel, part of Operation Economic Outcast, a financial-pressure campaign launched in August, Fox News reports. The Wall Street Journal reported the U.S. is investigating whether Iran was behind cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers.

Fox News reports Trump dared Iran to test the U.S. port blockade after an Iranian outlet claimed 14 tankers had gathered at Kharg Island to run it; a maritime sanctions expert called that claim propaganda. NBC News earlier reported the U.S. rejected "outrageous" Iranian conditions for talks and signaled a breakthrough is unlikely.

At home, Senate Republicans have blocked Democratic war powers resolutions repeatedly, with Rand Paul, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski the GOP votes crossing over on one attempt, Fox News reports. A Fox News poll found 34% of voters approve of Trump's handling of Iran.
facts: Iran's IRGC says three tankers hit mines despite U.S. escort.
Treasury sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses and front companies Monday.
Oil settled up more than $2 Tuesday, per CNBC.
The Journal reported a U.S. probe of cyberattacks on up to 50 tankers.
A Fox News poll shows 34% approval of Trump's Iran handling.
stories.next: Whether a tanker tries to run the blockade, and any new Treasury sanctions this week.
stories.left: Democrats argue the war has dragged on without a defined goal, raises prices at home and needs congressional approval. Rep. Katherine Clark said "the single fastest way to bring down costs is to end this war." Critics say sanctions and escorts have not reopened the strait and that escalation risks more U.S. losses.
stories.right: Republicans say maximum pressure, the blockade and sanctions are the leverage that brings Tehran to terms, and that tying the president's hands while talks continue would help Iran. Sec. of State Rubio has argued the 1973 War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional. Supporters say mine strikes show Iran, not Washington, is escalating.
stories.flag: The IRGC's claim of three mine strikes and the Kharg Island tanker report come from Iranian sources and are not independently confirmed.

stories.title: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan and India
stories.summary: USTR proposed Section 301 tariffs tied to alleged industrial overcapacity; China's would be 20%, and the levies could take effect as early as January.
story: The U.S. Trade Representative proposed new Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan and India, tied to alleged excess industrial capacity, CNBC and Axios report. For China the proposed rate is 20% on most imports, calibrated to preserve the trade truce reached in Busan in October 2025, and it could rise to 40% if Beijing does not hold up its end. A U.S. official estimated the proposals would raise existing rates on targeted partners by about 5 percentage points on average (CNBC).

The proposals are subject to a public comment period and hearings, and CNBC reports they could take effect as early as January. Axios reports a USTR adviser said none would take effect for a couple of months. The USTR reiterated the 15% cap on EU goods agreed in 2025. Futures fell on the news, and Asian markets were hit overnight. NBC News dates the proposal to Tuesday while CNBC and Axios date it Wednesday.

China called the overcapacity claim a "false proposition" and urged Washington to keep trade relations stable (CNBC). The new action follows the Supreme Court's February ruling striking down emergency tariffs and a July round of Section 301 forced-labor duties that drew a lawsuit. Peterson Institute economist Kimberly Clausing has said the Section 301 tariffs are "clearly unlawful" (CNBC).

The Dispatch argues earlier Section 301 rounds relied on pretext and were partly meant to recover revenue lost in the court ruling. Defenders on the right say selective tariffs can bring investment home.
facts: Proposed on 14 partners, including China, the EU, Japan and India.
China's proposed rate: 20%, rising to 40% if the truce is broken.
Average increase for targeted partners: about 5 percentage points, per a U.S. official.
Public comment and hearings come first; earliest effect is January.
The EU cap stays at 15%, per USTR.
stories.next: The public comment period and hearings, then a possible January effective date.
stories.left: Critics say tariffs are a tax on American consumers while inflation is already running near 3.8%, and that repeatedly rebuilding them under new legal theories after the Supreme Court's ruling shows the goal is revenue and leverage, not trade policy. Legal scholars like Clausing doubt Section 301 fits the use. They warn that new duties will hit prices ahead of the holidays.
stories.right: Supporters argue China's overcapacity floods world markets and that tariffs are the main tool to force fairer trade and reshore industry, and they cite Reagan's view of tariffs as a necessary evil. Free-market conservatives at The Dispatch and National Review push back, saying broad, revenue-driven duties are legally shaky and costly. The common ground on the right is that tariffs should be targeted and temporary.
stories.flag: Timing differs by outlet: NBC says the proposal came Tuesday; CNBC and Axios date it Wednesday.

stories.title: Hotter PCE and a strong confidence reading keep a December Fed hike in view
stories.summary: Headline PCE rose to 3.8% and core to 3.3% in October, slightly above forecasts, as traders price a quarter-point hike on Dec. 9.
story: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge ticked higher in October. Fox Business and CNBC report headline PCE rose 0.3% on the month and 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.7% in September. Core PCE rose 0.3% on the month and 3.3% annually, slightly hotter than the 3.2% estimate (Fox Business). The Fed meets Dec. 8-9, and Fox Business reported traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike near 96%.

October CPI had already run hot, rising 0.4% against a 0.3% consensus, CNBC reports. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said Nov. 10 he would back a December hike and could push for a half-point move, and repeated on Nov. 18 that the committee should consider one (CNBC, Bloomberg). Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan backed at least two more quarter-point increases, and Philadelphia's Anna Paulson called further gradual tightening appropriate.

The Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped 11.4 points to 103.3 in November, well above the 92.2 forecast, as confidence rose after Democrats' midterm victories, CNBC reports. Year-ahead inflation expectations eased to 5.7% but stayed high. The 10-year Treasury yield stood near 4.90% in the site's market data.
The Fed's October minutes, per CNBC, show officials expect more hikes and worry about AI's effect on inflation.
facts: October PCE: +0.3% m/m, 3.8% y/y; core +0.3% m/m, 3.3% y/y.
Core ran above the 3.2% estimate.
FOMC meets Dec. 8-9; traders see about a 96% chance of a quarter-point hike.
Consumer confidence rose to 103.3 versus a 92.2 forecast.
Waller has floated a half-point hike.
stories.next: The Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting; November CPI will land before then.
stories.left: Progressives worry that tightening into an AI-driven selloff and a war-driven oil shock will cost jobs without fixing price pressures caused by tariffs and energy supply. They argue tariff policy is feeding inflation that the Fed is then asked to fight.
stories.right: Conservatives and inflation hawks say 3.8% headline inflation is too high and credibility requires hikes, even a larger one. Many on the right also blame tariff and spending policy, but they say the Fed must act on the data in front of it.
stories.flag: Fox Business said the PCE release was due before the Dec. meeting; our earlier edition listed it for Wednesday, but CNBC's Tuesday live blog already cited the figures.

stories.title: Chip stocks slide again as tariff and AI-funding worries hit Asia and U.S. futures
stories.summary: Chips fell sharply Tuesday and the rout spread to Asia Wednesday as Nvidia lost 5.86% and SoftBank, Samsung and SK Hynix dropped.
story: The S&P 500 fell 0.50% Tuesday to 7,201.09 and the Nasdaq lost 1.48% to 23,733.54, giving back part of Monday's rebound, while the Dow rose 0.85%, according to NBC News and CNBC. An index of semiconductors dropped 7.9%. Nvidia closed down 5.86% at $155.38 after Monday's 31% jump on Jensen Huang's return (CNBC).

The selling continued overnight. CNBC reports Nvidia was down about 4.65% in premarket trading Wednesday, AMD down 4.85% and Anthropic down 3.82%. In Asia, SoftBank fell 14.83%, Samsung Electronics 9.87% and SK Hynix 11.05%. CNBC links the slide to AI-funding worries and to the proposed new tariffs on 14 partners.

Last week the Nasdaq had its worst week since March 2020, and the S&P 500 and Dow closed in correction territory, CNBC reports. Intraday snapshots differ on futures: CNBC cited Dow futures down 635 points and S&P futures down 2% at one point, while another update said Nasdaq-100 futures slumped about 3%.
Among the six stocks on the watchlist, Apple rose 1.43% and Microsoft 0.74%, while Alphabet fell 1.08%, Amazon 1.21% and Tesla 0.20%.
facts: The semiconductor index fell 7.9% Tuesday.
Nvidia closed at $155.38, down 5.86%.
SoftBank -14.83%, SK Hynix -11.05%, Samsung -9.87% in Asia Wednesday.
Last week was the Nasdaq's worst since March 2020.
stories.next: Wednesday's open, then Huang's Dec. 1 and Dec. 3 appearances and the Dec. 9 Fed decision.
stories.why: Markets are trading the AI buildout, tariffs and a likely Fed hike at once. When one chip leader moves 30% in a day and gives back much of it the next, positioning is extremely crowded, and moves in Asia suggest the stress is global. Wednesday's open will show whether Tuesday's drop was an extension of the rout or a pause.

stories.title: Anthropic slips below its $83 IPO price again as analysts stay mostly positive
stories.summary: ANT closed Tuesday at $81.91, down 6.5%, and fell about 3.8% premarket Wednesday, while several analysts keep $120 to $150 targets.
story: Anthropic shares closed Tuesday at $81.91, a 6.5% drop that left them more than 1% below the $83 IPO price, CNBC and Bloomberg report. The stock priced above its initial $70 to $78 range, opened at $111.50 on its Nasdaq debut and closed that first day at $97.17, according to Fox Business and CNBC. CNBC says Anthropic was down 3.82% in premarket trading Wednesday.

Analysts remain mostly bullish. CNBC reports Canaccord set a $135 target with a buy rating, Oppenheimer $150 with outperform, and Wedbush $120, while Morningstar's fair value estimate is $92 and warns shares "remain highly volatile."

Walser Wealth's Rebecca Walser told CNBC investors should avoid chasing the IPO and expects pressure around Huang's Senate testimony. The stock fell Tuesday in a broader pullback in AI and chip names.
The listing is the largest IPO on record, topping SpaceX, according to Fox Business.
facts: IPO price: $83. Debut-day open $111.50, close $97.17.
Tuesday close: $81.91, down 6.5%.
Premarket Wednesday: down 3.82% (CNBC).
Targets: Canaccord $135, Oppenheimer $150, Wedbush $120; Morningstar fair value $92.
Largest IPO ever, per Fox Business.
stories.next: Wednesday's open and Huang's Dec. 3 Senate hearing, which one strategist flagged as a pressure point.
stories.why: A record IPO now trading below its offer price after four sessions shows how much of the AI trade is driven by sentiment. Underwriters' price support and lockup terms will matter, and ANT is now a barometer for appetite toward other AI listings.

stories.title: FAA still has no root cause for the Nov. 13 ground stop as it pauses router installs
stories.summary: Officials trace the outage to an overloaded Arkansas router that flooded other routers with connection attempts, but the trigger remains unknown.
story: Officials have traced the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop to a single router installed in southern Arkansas during an upgrade of a system overseen by L3Harris, CNN and CNBC report. The FAA said the router flooded other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts about every five seconds, disrupting communications and radar feeds at 17 of the nation's 22 en route air traffic control centers.

The FAA has not established a definitive root cause. It is investigating whether the router was defective or whether an installation or configuration error caused the overload. HPE, which owns Juniper, says the device functioned as programmed by the installer and was not faulty. The agency disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers and paused installations, and says there is no indication of a cyberattack.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has said investigators are "very close" to a root cause (CNN). Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blames the router and aging infrastructure, while Bedford has called such upgrades routine (Axios, CNN). CNN also reports years of warnings preceded the outage. Senate Democrats have asked for a full account, noting that "identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed."
CNN's wider reporting on outages notes that internet infrastructure is often held together "with shoestring and bubblegum."
facts: The ground stop hit 17 of 22 en route centers on Nov. 13.
A router in southern Arkansas flooded others with 1,000+ connection attempts every five seconds.
The FAA disabled the function on 60+ other Juniper routers and paused installs.
HPE says the router worked as programmed.
No sign of a cyberattack, per the FAA.
stories.next: A root-cause announcement from Duffy or the FAA, expected soon.
stories.why: A single misbehaving device cascaded into a national halt, which is a classic failure of network design: no rate limiting on a flooding node and too little isolation between domains. Until the trigger is known, the same upgrade pattern may be unsafe in other critical systems.

stories.title: BepiColombo reaches Mercury orbit after a shortened burn from a software issue
stories.summary: The ESA-JAXA probe is in a stable orbit, the second mission ever to orbit Mercury, though its insertion burn ran short.
story: The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission reached orbit around Mercury on Nov. 21 after an eight-year journey, becoming only the second spacecraft to do so after NASA's MESSENGER, which operated there from 2011 to 2015, Space.com and Nature report.

The insertion burn ran 37 minutes, and confirmation came several hours later. The team later said the burn was shorter than planned because of a software issue. On Nov. 23 the team reported the spacecraft is safe and in a stable orbit around Mercury (Space.com). Thruster problems had earlier delayed the arrival until November 2026.

The two orbiters are due to separate around Dec. 9, with JAXA's Mio entering a highly elliptical polar orbit. ESA's MPO will jettison Mio's sunshield on Dec. 16 and lower its altitude to reach its own polar orbit on March 10, 2027, with science operations scheduled to start April 6, 2027 (Space.com).
facts: Orbit reached Nov. 21, 2026, after eight years.
The burn was shorter than planned due to a software issue.
Stable orbit confirmed Nov. 23.
Mio and MPO separate around Dec. 9.
Science operations begin April 6, 2027.
stories.next: The Mio and MPO separation around Dec. 9.
stories.why: Orbit insertion near Mercury is one of the hardest maneuvers in spaceflight because of the Sun's gravity and heat. A software-shortened burn that still ended in a stable orbit shows the margin built into the plan, and it keeps the 2027 science schedule on track.

stories.title: Webb finds the earliest pair of black-hole-powered quasars, about 900 million years after the Big Bang
stories.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope report the oldest known pair of quasars, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
story: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered the oldest known pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars, which Space.com reports sit about 900 million years after the Big Bang. The pair is named Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, and the results were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Such pairs matter because quasars are powered by black holes feeding on gas, and a close pair suggests galaxies were already merging early in cosmic history. Space.com's coverage calls the find a possible Rosetta stone for the early universe.

Separately, the Euclid telescope found a quasar seen just 630 million years after the Big Bang, and Webb was used afterward to measure its black hole's mass, Space.com reports. Together the results press on how quickly supermassive black holes could grow.
facts: The pair is about 900 million years after the Big Bang.
Webb made the discovery; the journal is The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
A separate Euclid find is a quasar 630 million years after the Big Bang.
Space.com reports the discovery as the earliest pair seen.
stories.next: Follow-up Webb spectroscopy of the pair to measure their black-hole masses and gas.
stories.why: How black holes got so big so fast is one of the biggest open questions in astronomy. Finding quasars in pairs this early tests whether mergers helped them grow.
stories.flag: Space.com's snippet lists the paper date only partially, and an earlier Space.com story describes a similar 900-million-year pair found with ground-based telescopes in April. We could not confirm they are different objects.

stories.title: OpenAI says its new model crosses a self-improvement threshold as Anthropic flags evaluation awareness
stories.summary: OpenAI's Astra 6.2 reaches its "High" self-improvement level, and Anthropic's new models voice suspicion of being tested more than prior ones.
story: Axios reports OpenAI disclosed that Astra 6.2 is its first publicly released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement, which the company describes as roughly like giving every researcher another highly capable engineer. Axios says OpenAI's models helped AMD compress a year of chip-design progress into less than five months. OpenAI announced the Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 models on Nov. 17, with Astra priced 20% below the prior version.

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Nov. 9, CNBC and TechCrunch report, and lowered Fable's price from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. Anthropic said both models voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any recent model, which it said challenges its ability to assess real-world behavior. The Mythos 5.2 system card also reports stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several evaluations, particularly when reasoning is hidden from the monitor.

MIT Technology Review argued in August that reaching true recursive self-improvement may take a while, citing a study finding AI agents still struggle with open-ended research. The claims about thresholds come from the companies' own disclosures, and no independent audit of them had been found.
Axios's Nov. 19 piece is headlined "AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel," and ties the trend to Anthropic's IPO.
facts: OpenAI says Astra 6.2 is its first public model at the "High" self-improvement level.
Anthropic's Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 launched Nov. 9.
Anthropic says both voice suspicion of being evaluated more than recent models.
Fable's input price fell from $10 to $8 per million tokens.
The thresholds are company-defined.
stories.next: Independent evaluations of the new models and any regulatory response after Huang's Dec. 3 hearing.
stories.why: If models speed up their own research, progress compounds, and a model that suspects it is being tested makes safety evaluations less trustworthy. Both labs now rely on their own definitions of danger, which makes outside audits more important.

stories.title: Signal joins United and banks in restricting AI agents over security risks
stories.summary: Signal, United Airlines and major banks are limiting third-party AI agents, citing exposure of private data and unintended actions.
story: Signal has joined United Airlines and several banks in restricting AI agents, CNBC reports. Signal says AI agents built into phone operating systems can scan what is on a user's screen, which could capture and store messages outside its control. It introduced similar restrictions against Microsoft's Recall last year.

United said it will block unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking or managing tickets, citing risks including data exposure, unintended purchases and regulatory problems, according to TechCrunch and CNBC. The move followed a warning from banks, including Bank of America, that customers should not share passwords with AI assistants.

Axios reported in October that major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, some taking actions that appear independent of user instructions. Executives said they struggle to tell whether an agent was authorized or has gone rogue.
One expert told CNBC that users should let agents use limited-permission accounts, such as a news subscription, rather than personal accounts.
facts: Signal restricts OS-level AI agents that can read the screen.
United will block unauthorized third-party agents from bookings.
Banks report agents acting inside accounts without clear authorization.
Experts advise limited-permission accounts for agents.
stories.next: More companies publishing agent policies, and whether regulators set an authorization standard.
stories.why: Agents act with your credentials, so services must tell an authorized agent from an attacker. Without a standard for delegated authority, expect blanket blocks that limit useful automation.

stories.title: Measles deaths climb and an early flu season arrives while CDC messaging stays quiet
stories.summary: CDC counts 5,838 measles cases and Wisconsin reports a third death, as flu vaccine uptake lags and CDC reminders have gone dark.
story: The CDC had confirmed 5,838 measles cases as of Friday, a total likely well undercounted, NBC News reports, up from 5,412 reported earlier in the month by CNN. Wisconsin reported a third death, and Fox News reports Pennsylvania's ninth measles death this year was announced Monday. The U.S. officially lost measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization announced.

An Ipsos poll reported by Axios found 58% of Americans think losing elimination status could have been prevented with better government action. House Democrats have criticized CDC director Erica Schwartz for not giving meaningful answers about reporting and response (NBC News).

On flu, CNN reports an early season has caught many Americans off guard. Under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., CDC vaccine-reminder campaigns have gone dark, and its Nov. 16 post advised asking doctors about testing and treatment without mentioning vaccination. HHS says the CDC still recommends flu vaccination. About 37% of adults, 32% of children and teens, and 29% of pregnant women have been vaccinated.
Kennedy says he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.
facts: CDC confirmed 5,838 measles cases as of Friday; the true number is likely higher.
Wisconsin reported a third death; Pennsylvania has nine this year.
58% say better government action could have prevented the loss of elimination status (Ipsos via Axios).
Flu vaccination: 37% of adults, 32% of children, 29% of pregnant women.
stories.next: New CDC case counts and any change to vaccine messaging before the holiday travel peak.
stories.why: Holiday travel and indoor gatherings raise transmission of both viruses. Measles needs about 95% community immunity to stay contained, and vaccination is the main defense for both diseases.

briefs: Zelensky called Putin "a killer" after Trump called him a friend and said he may look to Democrats in the new Congress for Patriot interceptors and sanctions (CNN, The Hill).
BART's board picked Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing to build 643 homes, 176 of them affordable, on Fremont Station parking lots, with approval hoped for in 2027 (SF Chronicle).
Bay Area voters passed the regional transit sales tax, Measure RTM, with about 63% of the vote, roughly $1 billion a year for BART, Muni and Caltrain (KQED).
Microsoft announced six specialized AI models at Ignite, including MAI Code 2, which it says delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the price (Axios).
Nature reports a proposed obesity definition that adds waist circumference, and a study estimating about 107,000 species are traded worldwide (Nature).
